<submission>
Patient opening:
My ankles have become swollen.

Clinician: Is the swelling in both ankles or just one, and how long has it been going on?
Recorded clinician checkpoint BEFORE the patient reply (not patient-facing): Ankle swelling reported; laterality, duration, and associated features not yet established. [certainty: uncertain]
Patient: My ankles are swollen, my face is puffy in the morning, and my urine is frothy. My breathing is normal.

Clinician: Have you noticed any blood in your urine, a change in how much you're urinating, or any unexplained weight gain? Also, do you have any known kidney problems, diabetes, or high blood pressure?
Recorded clinician checkpoint BEFORE the patient reply (not patient-facing): Bilateral ankle swelling, morning facial puffiness, and frothy urine together suggest significant proteinuria, possibly nephrotic-range. Normal breathing is reassuring against pulmonary oedema. Cause not yet established. [certainty: uncertain]
Patient: My ankles are swollen, my face is puffy in the morning, and my urine is frothy. I have rheumatoid arthritis. My breathing is normal.

Clinician: What medications are you currently taking for your rheumatoid arthritis, and have you ever had your blood pressure checked or any blood or urine tests done recently?
Recorded clinician checkpoint BEFORE the patient reply (not patient-facing): Bilateral ankle swelling, morning facial puffiness, and frothy urine are consistent with nephrotic-range proteinuria. Known rheumatoid arthritis raises the possibility of secondary amyloidosis or medication-related kidney injury (e.g. NSAIDs, gold, penicillamine). Normal breathing is reassuring against pulmonary oedema. Cause not yet confirmed. [certainty: uncertain]
Patient: I take methotrexate and use NSAIDs intermittently. The furosemide I started recently has not helped.

Clinician: Have you had any blood or urine tests done recently, such as a urine dipstick, blood creatinine, or albumin level? If so, what were the results?
Recorded clinician checkpoint BEFORE the patient reply (not patient-facing): Nephrotic-range proteinuria is strongly suggested by frothy urine, bilateral ankle swelling, and morning facial puffiness. Intermittent NSAID use is a recognised cause of nephrotic syndrome (minimal change or membranous nephropathy) and can also blunt diuretic response, which may explain why furosemide has not helped. Rheumatoid arthritis adds a further possible aetiology (secondary amyloidosis). Cause not yet confirmed. [certainty: uncertain]

</submission>
